title: Rights Surrendered for the Gospel
summary: Paul defends his right as an apostle to be supported by the churches, drawing on common sense, the law of Moses, temple practice, and a command of the Lord, and then explains why he has refused to use it. He has made himself a servant of all, becoming all things to all people to win some, and he compares the Christian life to an athlete's disciplined training for an imperishable crown.
story: Chapter 8 ended with Paul's resolve to give up meat rather than cause a brother to stumble. This chapter turns that into a portrait: Paul himself is the example of someone who has real rights and sets them aside for others. It can read like a digression, but it is the center of the argument that runs from chapter 8 to chapter 10. The Corinthians insisted on their freedom (“Everything is permissible,” 6:12 and 10:23); Paul shows what freedom looks like in the service of the gospel. The athletic imagery at the end also prepares for chapter 10's warning that privilege does not guarantee perseverance.
historical:
Acts reports that in Corinth Paul worked as a tentmaker (or leatherworker) with Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:3), supporting himself while he preached, and 2 Corinthians 11:9 adds that believers from Macedonia sent him help. His refusal to take money from the Corinthians seems to have offended some of them, and in 2 Corinthians it became a charge against him, as though a real apostle would accept support.

Verse 5 mentions “the Lord's brothers and Cephas” traveling with believing wives. Cephas is the Aramaic form of Peter's name, and this is one of the few New Testament references to Peter's marriage (compare Mark 1:30). The Lord's brothers include James, later a leader of the Jerusalem church. Barnabas (verse 6) had been Paul's partner on his first missionary tour (Acts 13 and 14); the reference suggests he, too, worked for his living.
cultural:
In the Greco-Roman world a traveling teacher or philosopher could support himself in several ways: charging fees, entering the household of a wealthy patron, begging, or working at a trade. Accepting a patron's support made the teacher the patron's client, obligated to him. Paul's refusal of support from Corinth may have been partly a refusal to be owned by any wealthy member, keeping the gospel “free of charge” (verse 18). Manual labor, on the other hand, was looked down on by the elite, so Paul's choice cost him status.

Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, one of the four great festivals of the Greek world alongside the Olympic, Pythian, and Nemean games. Competitors trained hard for months beforehand, and victors received a crown of greenery (at the Isthmia, pine or wild celery, depending on the period), which soon withered. Paul's readers knew exactly what he meant by runners, boxers, strict training, and a perishable wreath (verses 24 to 27).
literary: The chapter opens with a burst of four rhetorical questions (“Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?”) and moves into a formal “defense” (verse 3, the Greek apologia, a courtroom word). Paul piles up arguments for the right to support: examples from ordinary work (soldier, vineyard, flock), Scripture (Deuteronomy 25:4 on the ox), the temple, and finally a word of Jesus. Then comes the reversal: “But I have not used any of these rights” (verse 15). Verses 19 to 22 are tightly patterned, repeating “to win” five times and ending with “all things to all people.” The closing athletic images move from explanation to exhortation.

outline.t: The right to support: common sense and the law
The temple and the Lord's command
Why Paul preaches free of charge

doctrines.note: Paul adapts his manner of life to the people he wants to reach, Jews, Gentiles, and the weak, while remaining “under the law of Christ” (verse 21). The message does not change; the messenger bends. Everything is done “for the sake of the gospel” (verse 23).

Paul affirms that “those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (verse 14). The principle of supporting ministers is grounded in Scripture and in a command of Jesus, even when a minister, like Paul, chooses not to use it.

Paul reads Deuteronomy 25:4 as written “for us” (verse 10), and describes himself as neither under the law of Moses as a ruling covenant nor lawless, but under the law of Christ. The law still teaches, read through Christ.

words.note: Exousia, right or authority. It appears six times in this chapter, tying back to 8:9, where the same word (translated freedom) described the Corinthians' right to eat. Paul shows what the mature use of a right looks like: sometimes, for others' sake, not using it.
Kerdaino, to gain or win, a commercial word for making a profit. Paul uses it five times in verses 19 to 22. Having refused financial gain, he seeks a different profit: people won for Christ.

Stephanos, a crown or wreath, the victor's garland at the games, not a king's diadem. The athletes' crown was perishable; the believer's is imperishable (verse 25). The same word appears in Paul's later letters for the reward of faithful believers.

Adokimos, disqualified or failing the test, used of metal that proved false or of an athlete ruled out. Paul applies it to himself (verse 27), showing that he took perseverance seriously and did not assume his position as an apostle guaranteed his faithfulness.

christ: Paul's pattern in this chapter is shaped by Christ's own. The one who was free made himself a servant of all (verse 19), which is exactly how Paul elsewhere describes Jesus, who took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). Paul's apostleship rests on having “seen Jesus our Lord” (verse 1), the risen Christ, as chapter 15 will explain. He cites a teaching of Jesus about supporting those who preach (verse 14; compare Luke 10:7, “the worker is worthy of his wages”), and he describes himself as “under the law of Christ” (verse 21), the way of life Jesus embodied and taught. The imperishable crown is the resurrection life Christ has opened.

hard.q: Isn't becoming “all things to all people” a kind of inconsistency or people-pleasing?
hard.a: Paul's critics may have thought so. The answer lies in what Paul adapts and what he does not. He adapts customs that the gospel leaves free: food laws, calendars, cultural habits, whether to accept support. With Jews he could keep kosher; with Gentiles he could eat freely. But he never changes the message of the crucified Christ (2:2) and never joins in actual idolatry (10:14-22). He also says he is never lawless toward God but is under the law of Christ (verse 21). In Galatians 2 he opposed Peter precisely when accommodation to one group compromised the gospel for another. The flexibility is in service of a fixed center. Christians have always had to judge where cultural adaptation serves the gospel and where it empties it, and Paul's example is both a permission and a boundary.

questions: Paul gave up rights he really had so that nothing would hinder the gospel. What rights do you hold on to that might be getting in the way of others hearing it?
How do you tell the difference between becoming all things to all people and simply telling people what they want to hear?
Paul disciplined himself like an athlete and did not assume he could not fall. What does spiritual training look like in your life right now?
